content: The provided text is a detailed list of drug interactions involving levonorgestrel intrauterine systems (IUS) and various other medications. 1. Larotrectinib: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4, which is involved in levonorgestrel metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is currently unknown. 2. Levoketoconazole: This drug can elevate the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical relevance of this interaction remains uncertain. 3. Acetazolamide: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by altering CYP3A4-mediated metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 4. Amobarbital: This drug decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Close monitoring is recommended when these drugs are co-administered. 5. Anastrozole: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 6. Antithrombin Alfa: Co-administration with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may result in pharmacodynamic antagonism, reducing the effects of both drugs. This combination should be avoided or alternative therapies should be used due to the risk of thromboembolic disorders. 7. Antithrombin III: Similar to antithrombin alfa, this interaction may lead to reduced efficacy of both drugs through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid this combination or use alternative therapies due to the risk of thromboembolic events. 8. Apalutamide: This drug decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 9. Argatroban: Co-administration with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may result in pharmacodynamic antagonism, reducing the effects of both drugs. Avoid this combination or use alternative therapies due to the risk of thromboembolic disorders. 10. Atazanavir: This medication may either increase or decrease levonorgestrel levels in intrauterine systems by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. If possible, consider alternative treatments. 11. Bemiparin: Co-administration with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may result in pharmacodynamic antagonism, reducing the effects of both drugs. Avoid this combination or use alternative therapies due to the risk of thromboembolic disorders. 12. Bivalirudin: Similar to bemiparin, this interaction may lead to reduced efficacy of both drugs through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid this combination or use alternative therapies due to the risk of thromboembolic events. 13. Bosentan: This drug decreases the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 14. Carbamazepine: This medication reduces levonorgestrel levels in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 15. Cenobamate: This drug decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems through an unspecified mechanism, likely involving CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Women should be advised to use additional or alternative non-hormonal contraceptive methods when using cenobamate. 16. Ceritinib: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 17. Clobazam: This drug decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by weakly inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive effectiveness may be diminished. Additional non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 18. Cobicistat: This medication increases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 19. Crofelermer: This drug increases levonorgestrel levels in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 in the gastrointestinal tract. However, systemic inhibition is unlikely due to minimal absorption. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 20. Cyclophosphamide: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 21. Cyclosporine: Co-administration with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may increase cyclosporine levels by reducing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 22. Dabrafenib: This drug decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 23. Dalteparin: Co-administration with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may result in pharmacodynamic antagonism, reducing the effects of both drugs. Avoid this combination or use alternative therapies due to the risk of thromboembolic disorders. 24. Danazol: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 25. Dexamethasone: This drug decreases the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 26. Drospirenone: This medication may increase the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 27. Efavirenz: This drug decreases the levels of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 28. Elagolix: Levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may reduce the efficacy of elagolix through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Estrogen-containing contraceptives are expected to reduce elagolix efficacy. Women should use non-hormonal contraceptives during and for one week after elagolix treatment. 29. Encorafenib: This drug decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel in intrauterine systems by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. Women of childbearing potential should use highly effective non-hormonal contraception during and for two weeks after treatment. 30. Enoxaparin: Co-administration with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems may result in pharmacodynamic antagonism, reducing the effects of both drugs. Avoid this combination or use alternative therapies due to the risk of thromboembolic disorders.
